unit.title: Use workshop machines for basic operations

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Who may use a workshop machine at the Centre?
options: Anyone who has watched someone else use it
Only people trained and allowed to use it
Anyone, as long as they wear safety glasses
Only the person who is fastest at the job

questions.stem: Why must all machine guards be in place before a machine is started?
options: To keep hands, clothing and chips away from moving parts
To make the machine run more quietly and smoothly
To stop dust and dirt getting into the machine's motor
To make the machine look neat for visitors

questions.stem: Why should you not wear gloves when using a pedestal drill?
options: A turning drill can catch a glove and pull your hand in
Gloves make it hard to read the speed chart on the machine
Gloves wear out quickly on the drill table
Gloves stop the cutting fluid from working

questions.stem: What should you do with rings, watches and loose sleeves before using a machine?
options: Keep them on, but work more slowly and carefully
Remove them or secure them so they cannot be caught
Wrap them in tape so that they do not get scratched
Only remove them if the supervisor asks you to

questions.stem: Before switching on a machine, what should you check?
options: That the machine is painted and looks clean
That the radio in the workshop is turned off
That guards are fitted and keys are removed
That someone else used the machine that morning

questions.stem: A machine makes a strange noise and smells hot while it is running. What should you do?
options: Stop it, isolate it, and report it to the supervisor
Carry on, as most machines make some noise
Pour some cutting fluid on the motor to cool it down
Turn the speed up to clear the problem

questions.stem: Why must you never leave a machine running when you walk away from it?
options: Someone else could be hurt by the moving parts
The machine will slowly use up all the cutting fluid
The speed setting will change by itself
The machine will cool down too much

questions.stem: Kemar wants to move the belt to a slower speed on a belt-driven pedestal drill. What must he do first?
options: Open the cover while the drill is running slowly
Hold the pulley still with his hand
Ask a friend to press the stop button for him
Switch off, isolate and wait for it to stop

questions.stem: How should a small piece of steel plate be held for drilling on a pedestal drill?
options: In your hand, pressed firmly on the table
Against the column with one finger
Clamped in a machine vice or to the table
Loose on the table, as the drill holds it down

questions.stem: What can happen if the work is not clamped when drilling?
options: The hole will come out larger and neater
The drill will cut faster and stay cooler
The cutting fluid will not reach the drill
The work can grab and spin round dangerously

questions.stem: How does the drill size affect the speed you should set on a pedestal drill?
options: Larger drills need a faster speed
All drill sizes use the same speed
Larger drills need a slower speed
Smaller drills need a slower speed

questions.stem: Why is cutting fluid used when drilling mild steel?
options: To colour the hole so it can be seen
To cool the drill and help it cut cleanly
To make the metal soft before drilling
To stop the chuck from turning too fast

questions.stem: How should metal chips be cleared from the drill table?
options: With your bare hand, once the drill stops
By blowing them away with your mouth
With a brush, after the drill has stopped
With a rag while the drill is still turning

questions.stem: As the drill is about to break through the bottom of the hole, what should you do?
options: Push down harder to finish quickly
Lift your hand off the work
Ease off the feed pressure
Change to a larger drill

questions.stem: Why is a centre punch mark made before drilling?
options: To make the drill cut a larger hole
To mark the metal so the supervisor can see it
To harden the steel at that point
To guide the drill point so it does not wander

questions.stem: Andre has drilled a 10 mm hole and its edge is sharp and rough. What should he do?
options: Remove the burr with a deburring tool
Leave it, as burrs fall off with use
Hit the edge flat with a hammer
Fill it with paint to make it smooth

questions.stem: Which part of a pedestal drill is raised, lowered or swung round to bring the work to the right height?
options: The pulley
The table
The chuck
The motor

questions.stem: Why is the work set over a hole in the table, or on parallel packing, when drilling right through?
options: So that the machine vice is not needed at all
So the cutting fluid can drain away
So that the drill runs more slowly
So the drill does not cut into the table

questions.stem: On a pedestal grinder, what is the largest safe gap between the wheel and the rest that supports the work?
options: About 3 mm or less
About 10 mm
About 25 mm
Any gap, if you hold the work tightly

questions.stem: What must you wear when using a pedestal grinder, even if the machine has an eye shield?
options: Leather welding gloves only
Ear muffs only
Nothing extra is needed
Safety glasses or goggles

questions.stem: Why should you stand to one side when you first switch on a pedestal grinder?
options: So you can read the speed on the label
In case a damaged wheel breaks as it speeds up
So the sparks can go into the dust bin
So the motor gets more air to cool it

questions.stem: Why should you not grind on the flat side of a normal (straight) grinding wheel?
options: It makes the wheel spin the wrong way
The wheel is not made for it and can break
It gives too smooth a finish for steel
It uses too much electricity

questions.stem: Why should you not grind aluminium or other soft metals on a normal steel-grinding wheel?
options: They are too hard and blunt the wheel at once
They make the grinder run much faster
They turn the wheel a different colour
They clog the wheel, which can then break

questions.stem: A small steel part gets very hot while it is being ground. What is a safe way to keep it cool?
options: Hold it with a wet cloth wrapped round your hand
Dip it in the water pot from time to time
Grind faster so the heat has no time to build
Press it harder onto the wheel

questions.stem: Before a new wheel is fitted to a pedestal grinder, why must its speed rating be checked?
options: So that it matches the colour of the guard
So it is safe at the speed the grinder runs
So that it can be used on both sides
So the grinder can run without a guard

questions.stem: Before cutting on a bandsaw, how should the upper blade guide be set?
options: As high as it will go, to see the blade
Touching the work so it holds it down
Just above the work, as close as possible
Taken off, so the blade can move freely

questions.stem: Delroy has to cut a 3 m length of steel tube on a horizontal bandsaw. What should he do with the long end?
options: Let it hang over the end of the saw freely
Support it on a roller stand at the right height
Ask a friend to hold the end up in their hands
Tie the long end to the saw frame with wire

questions.stem: Why must the work be clamped tightly in the saw's vice before cutting?
options: So the blade can cut on both strokes
So that less cutting fluid is needed
So it cannot move and break the blade
So that the saw runs at a lower speed

questions.stem: What is the danger of a bandsaw blade that is too loose?
options: It will cut a much straighter line
It will make the motor run backwards
It will stop the coolant pump working
It can slip off the wheels or snap

questions.stem: Marsha uses an abrasive cut-off saw (chop saw) to cut angle iron. What must she check about the sparks?
options: That they fly away from people and things that burn
That they are pointed towards the nearest wall socket
That they land in the rag bin next to the saw
That they hit the floor close to her own feet

questions.stem: Why must a chop saw's disc stop fully before the cut piece is taken out?
options: So that the motor can rest between each cut
So the disc can be turned over
So the guard can be lifted off
So the moving disc cannot cut your hand

questions.stem: On a horizontal bandsaw, why is the blade allowed to come down slowly onto the work?
options: So the blade cuts on its way back up
So less of the blade is used
So the teeth are not broken or stripped
So the work does not need clamping

questions.stem: How should a bandsaw be cleaned after use?
options: Switch off and isolate, then use a brush
Run it and hold a rag on the blade
Wash it down with water from a hose pipe
Wipe the moving blade with your hand

questions.stem: What must the tip of a lathe cutting tool be level with?
options: The top of the tool post
The bottom edge of the chuck jaws
The centre height of the work
The top of the tailstock

questions.stem: What should you do before measuring work that is held in a lathe?
options: Slow the lathe down to a low speed
Measure it carefully while it turns
Wipe it with a rag while it turns
Stop the lathe fully first

questions.stem: Which lathe operation makes the diameter of a bar smaller along its length?
options: Drilling
Turning
Knurling
Parting off

questions.stem: Why must the chuck key never be left in a lathe chuck?
options: It will get lost among the metal chips
It can be thrown out when the lathe starts
It will make the jaws grip too tightly
It stops the coolant from reaching the work

questions.stem: Long, stringy metal chips are wrapping round the work on the lathe. After stopping the lathe, what should be used to remove them?
options: A chip hook or a brush
Your bare fingers
A rag held against the work
A screwdriver while the work turns

questions.stem: Why is the lathe speed set lower for a large-diameter bar than for a small one?
options: Large bars are lighter and spin easily
Small bars need less cutting fluid
A large bar's edge moves faster at the same speed
The chuck is only able to grip large bars at slow speeds

questions.stem: When using a guillotine to cut sheet metal, where must your fingers be?
options: Behind the finger guard, away from the blade
Under the hold-down clamps to keep the sheet flat
On the cutting line to guide the blade
Anywhere, as long as you cut slowly

questions.stem: Why must you never cut steel thicker than the guillotine's rated capacity?
options: The cut edge will be too smooth for welding
The sheet will be too light to handle
It uses too much power from the mains
It can damage the blade and the machine

questions.stem: After machining, how should you check that the part is correct?
options: Hold it up and guess whether it looks right
Measure it and compare it with the drawing
Ask a friend if it looks about right
Weigh it on the scale in the store

questions.stem: A drawing says a hole is 10 mm ± 0.2 mm. Which measured size is acceptable?
options: 9.7 mm

questions.stem: Who should oil and grease the moving parts of a machine?
options: A trained person, following the maker's instructions
Anyone at all, using whatever oil can be found
Only the customer who owns the job being done
Nobody, as these machines never need any oiling

questions.stem: At the end of a session on the pedestal drill, what should you do?
options: Leave the chips on the table for the next class
Leave the drill in the chuck and the power on
Switch off, clean the machine and return the tools
Pour cutting fluid all over the machine to stop rust

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name of the red, mushroom-shaped button that stops a machine at once in an emergency?
What is the trade name for the chips and curls of metal cut off by a drill or a lathe?
What is the usual point angle, in degrees, of a general-purpose twist drill?
What is the name of the tool used to clean and true up the face of a grinding wheel?
What do we call the cone-shaped recess cut at the top of a hole so that a flat-headed screw sits level with the surface?
What is the name of the lathe chuck whose three jaws all move together to centre round work?
Which lathe operation makes the end of a bar flat and square to its length?
What is the name of the part of a pedestal grinder that supports the work close to the wheel?
Which grey, brittle metal, often used for machine beds and bases, is usually drilled and machined dry?
What do we call cutting off the power and locking the switch so that a machine cannot be started while someone works on it?
On a vertical bandsaw, which way should the teeth of the blade point?
What is the name of the test done by lightly tapping a grinding wheel and listening, to check that it is not cracked?
What do we call the small first hole drilled to guide a larger drill?
What is the name of the device on a pedestal drill that stops the drill going deeper than a set amount?
What is the name of the tool used after drilling to make a hole smooth and exactly to size?

essays.stem: Describe the general safety rules you must follow before and while using any workshop machine.
essays.modelAnswer: Before using a machine I must be trained on it and have the supervisor's permission. I read the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules for that machine. I wear safety glasses and safety boots, and ear protection if it is noisy. I remove rings and watches, button my sleeves and tie back long hair. I do not wear gloves near turning spindles or chucks. I check the machine: guards in place, emergency stop working, no damage, and the area clear and dry. I make sure the work and the tool are held firmly and the chuck key is removed. While the machine runs, I stay at it, keep my hands away from moving parts and never reach over it. I do not talk to or distract other operators. I stop the machine before measuring, cleaning or adjusting anything. If something is wrong, I stop, isolate the machine and report it.
markingPoints: Trained and permitted; follows the maker's instructions and Centre rules
Correct PPE; no jewellery, loose clothing or gloves near turning parts; hair tied back
Pre-start checks: guards, emergency stop, condition, clear and dry area
Work and tool held firmly; keys removed
While running: stays at the machine, hands clear, stops before measuring or adjusting, reports faults

essays.stem: Describe how to set up and drill a 10 mm hole through a 6 mm steel plate on a pedestal drill, from marking out to cleaning up.
essays.modelAnswer: I read the drawing and mark the hole centre with two crossing scribed lines, then centre punch it. I put on safety glasses, remove rings and tie back my hair, and I wear no gloves. I check the drill: guard on, table firm, belt cover closed. I clamp the plate in a machine vice with parallel packing under it, so the drill will break through into a gap and not into the vice or table. I fit a pilot drill of about 4 to 5 mm in the chuck, tighten it and remove the chuck key. I set a suitable speed from the chart, isolating the machine first if the belt must be moved. I line the drill up with the punch mark and drill the pilot hole with a steady feed and cutting fluid, easing off at break-through. Then I fit the 10 mm drill, set a slower speed and drill to size. I stop the machine, deburr both sides and check the hole. Finally I brush away the chips, clean the table and put the tools away.
markingPoints: Marks out with crossing lines and a centre punch
PPE (no gloves) and checks on the machine
Clamps the plate in a machine vice with packing underneath
Pilot hole first; speed from the chart, slower for the larger drill; isolates for belt changes; key removed
Steady feed with cutting fluid, eases off at break-through, deburrs, checks and cleans up

essays.stem: Explain why the spindle speed must suit the drill size and the material, and what happens if the speed is too fast or too slow.
essays.modelAnswer: Each material has a cutting speed that suits it: the speed at which the cutting edge should pass over the metal. The outer edge of a large drill travels further in each turn than that of a small drill, so at the same spindle speed it moves faster over the metal. That is why large drills need a slower spindle speed and small drills a faster one. Hard materials, such as tool steel, also need slower speeds than soft materials such as aluminium. If the speed is too fast, the drill overheats, its cutting edges burn and go blunt, it may turn blue, and the hole can come out rough or oversize. The drill may even break. If the speed is too slow, the job takes much longer, small drills can snap because too much pressure is used, and the finish can be poor. The right speed is taken from the chart on the machine or the maker's table, and cutting fluid is used to keep the drill cool.
markingPoints: Explains cutting speed: the speed of the cutting edge over the metal
Large drills need slower spindle speeds; small drills faster
Harder materials need slower speeds than soft ones
Too fast: overheating, blunt or burnt drill, poor hole; too slow: slow work, broken small drills, poor finish
Use the machine's speed chart and cutting fluid

essays.stem: Describe the checks you would make on a pedestal grinder before use, and how to use it safely to grind a chamfer on the end of a steel bar.
essays.modelAnswer: First I make sure I am allowed to use the grinder. I check the wheel for cracks, chips or other damage, and that it is the right type for steel. The wheel guards must be fitted and the eye shield must be clean and in place. I check that the gap between the wheel and the work rest is small, about 3 mm or less, and if it needs moving I adjust it only with the machine switched off and isolated. I check that the wheel face is not clogged or uneven; if it is, it is dressed by a trained person. I put on safety glasses or goggles, tie back my hair and remove loose items. I stand to one side, switch on, and let it run up to speed for a short time. To grind the chamfer, I rest the bar on the work rest and hold it firmly at about 45° to the wheel. I move it gently across the face of the wheel with light pressure, never using the side. I dip the bar in water to keep it cool. When I finish, I switch off and let the wheel stop.
markingPoints: Checks the wheel for damage and correct type; guards and eye shield in place
Work rest gap small (about 3 mm or less), adjusted only with the machine isolated
Safety glasses or goggles; stands to one side when starting
Holds the bar firmly on the rest at the chamfer angle, light pressure, face of the wheel only
Cools the work in water; switches off and lets the wheel stop

essays.stem: Describe how to cut a length of steel bar to size on a horizontal bandsaw or a power hacksaw.
essays.modelAnswer: First I check the drawing or cutting list for the length and the number of pieces. I check the saw: the blade is correctly tensioned and not damaged, the guards are fitted, the coolant is topped up if it is used, and the area is clear. I wear safety glasses and boots, with sleeves and hair secured. I mark the length on the bar, measuring from a square end and allowing for the width of the cut. I place the bar in the saw's vice, line up the mark with the blade and clamp it tightly. A long bar is supported on a roller stand at the same height. I set the blade guide close to the work. I switch on and let the blade come down slowly and steadily onto the work, without forcing it. When the cut is finished and the machine has stopped, I take out the piece, which may be hot and sharp. I deburr it and check its length. When all the pieces are cut, I clean the saw with a brush.
markingPoints: Checks the cutting list and the saw (blade, tension, guards, coolant)
Wears PPE and keeps sleeves and hair secured
Measures from a square end and allows for the width of the cut
Clamps tightly, supports long bar, sets the guide close, lets the blade feed down steadily
Waits for it to stop, handles the hot sharp piece carefully, deburrs, checks length, cleans the saw

essays.stem: Describe the main parts of a centre lathe and say what each one does.
essays.modelAnswer: The bed is the strong base of the lathe. It has flat or shaped slides on top, called ways, that the other parts move along. The headstock is at the left end. It holds the drive, the gears or belts for changing speed, and the spindle, which turns the work. The chuck is fitted to the spindle and grips the work in its jaws. The tailstock is at the right end and slides along the bed. It can hold a centre to support long work, or a drill chuck for drilling into the end of the work. The carriage, or saddle, moves along the bed and carries the cross slide, which moves the tool in and out across the work, and the top slide, which can be set at an angle for short tapers. The tool post holds the cutting tool. The lead screw and feed shaft can move the carriage by power for turning and screw cutting. Guards and an emergency stop protect the operator.
markingPoints: Bed with ways, and headstock with the spindle that turns the work
Chuck grips the work
Tailstock supports long work or holds a drill chuck
Carriage (saddle) with cross slide and top slide to move the tool
Tool post holds the tool; lead screw or feed shaft gives power feed; guards and emergency stop

essays.stem: Explain what isolating a machine means, and when and how it must be done.
essays.modelAnswer: Isolating a machine means cutting it off from its power supply so that it cannot start. Pressing the stop button is not enough, because someone could press the start button again. A machine must be isolated before opening covers to change belts or speeds, changing blades, drills or wheels, clearing a jam, cleaning inside the guards, adjusting guards or work rests, and before any repair. To isolate it, I switch off the machine, then switch off at the isolating switch or unplug it, and wait for all moving parts to stop. Where the Centre uses lock-off, I fit my own lock and a tag with my name and the date to the isolator, so nobody can switch it back on. I try the start button to prove the machine will not start, and return it to off. Only when the work is finished and the guards are back in place do I remove my lock and tag and restore the power.
markingPoints: Isolating means cutting off the power supply so the machine cannot start
The stop button alone is not enough
When: changing belts, blades or wheels, clearing jams, cleaning or adjusting inside guards, repairs
How: switch off, isolate or unplug, wait for parts to stop, lock and tag
Prove it will not start; remove lock only when finished and guards are back

essays.stem: Explain why cutting fluid is used, and how to handle cutting fluid and metal chips safely.
essays.modelAnswer: Cutting fluid cools the drill, blade or tool and the work, so the cutting edge does not overheat and go blunt. It also lubricates, so the tool cuts more easily and leaves a better finish, and it helps wash chips away from the cut. To handle it safely, I use only the fluid supplied, mixed as the maker says, and put it on with a brush or the machine's pump, not by hand near moving parts. I keep skin contact as low as possible, wash my hands after work, and report any skin rash. If I handle containers of fluid away from turning machines, I wear suitable gloves. Spills are wiped up at once so nobody slips, and old fluid goes in the right waste container, never down the drain. Metal chips are sharp and often hot. I never touch them with bare hands or blow them away. I stop the machine, use a brush or chip hook, and put the chips in the scrap bin.
markingPoints: Cools the tool and work so the edge does not overheat
Lubricates for easier cutting and a better finish, and washes chips away
Safe handling: maker's mix, applied by brush or pump, little skin contact, wash hands
Spills wiped up; old fluid disposed of correctly, not down the drain
Chips are hot and sharp: machine stopped, brush or chip hook, scrap bin

essays.stem: Compare a bandsaw, a power hacksaw and an abrasive cut-off saw for cutting steel. Say what each is good for and give one safety point for each.
essays.modelAnswer: A bandsaw has a long blade in a loop that runs one way round two wheels. It cuts steel bar, tube and sections cleanly and quietly, with little waste, and it is good for cutting many pieces to the same length. A safety point is to set the blade guide close to the work and keep hands away from the moving blade. A power hacksaw has a straight blade that moves back and forth like a hand hacksaw. It is simple and cheap to run, but slow, because it cuts on only one stroke. A safety point is to clamp the work tightly and keep clear of the moving frame. An abrasive cut-off saw, or chop saw, uses a thin abrasive disc. It cuts quickly and can cut hard steel, but it is noisy, throws sparks and leaves a hot, rough edge with burrs. Safety points are to check the disc's speed rating, use screens, point the sparks away from people and anything that can burn, and wear a face shield and ear protection.
markingPoints: Bandsaw: clean, quiet, little waste, good for repeat lengths; safety point (guide close, hands clear)
Power hacksaw: simple but slow; safety point (clamp tightly, keep clear of the frame)
Abrasive cut-off saw: fast, cuts hard steel, but noisy, sparks and burrs
Cut-off saw safety: disc speed rating, screens, sparks away from people and things that burn
Correct PPE named, such as face shield and ear protection

essays.stem: Explain why a machine and the area around it must be kept clean and tidy, and describe what you would do at the end of a machining session.
essays.modelAnswer: A clean, tidy machine area is safer and helps good work. Chips and oil on the floor can make people slip or cut themselves, and offcuts or tools left lying about can be tripped over or fall into moving parts. Chips left on a drill table or lathe bed stop the work sitting flat, so holes and cuts come out wrong, and they can damage the slides. A tidy area also means tools are easy to find, so time is saved. At the end of a session I switch off and isolate the machine. I remove drills, keys and cutting tools and put them back in their places. I brush the chips off the machine and table, never using my hands or blowing them at people, and put them in the scrap bin. I wipe off the cutting fluid and oil bare steel surfaces as the Centre requires. I sweep the floor and wipe up spills. Offcuts go in the scrap bin and finished parts in the labelled place, and I report any faults to the supervisor.
markingPoints: Safety reasons: slips, cuts, trips, items falling into moving parts
Quality and care reasons: chips stop work sitting flat and damage slides; tools easy to find
End of session: switch off, isolate, remove and return tools
Brush chips (not hands or air), wipe and oil the machine, sweep and clean spills
Sort scrap and finished parts; report faults

practical1.title: Mark out and drill a hole pattern on a pedestal drill
practical1.brief: Each member of the group marks out and drills a steel plate to the assessor's drawing using the pedestal drill. The plate is mild steel, about 100 mm × 50 mm × 6 mm, with four 8 mm holes (one near each corner) and one 10 mm hole in the centre, countersunk on one side. First, as a group, read the drawing, carry out the machine's pre-start checks with the assessor and fill in the check sheet. Then each member in turn: (1) marks out the hole centres with a rule, square and scriber and centre punches them; (2) clamps the plate in the machine vice with packing underneath; (3) chooses the speeds from the speed chart and has the assessor check them; (4) drills a pilot hole and then each hole to size, with cutting fluid; (5) countersinks the centre hole and deburrs all the holes; (6) checks the hole positions against the drawing. While one member drills, another stands by the emergency stop as a watcher, and the rest check the finished plates. Photograph each stage and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: One mild steel plate, about 100 mm × 50 mm × 6 mm, for each member
The assessor's drawing and the drill's speed chart
Pedestal drill with a machine vice and parallel packing
HSS twist drills (4 mm, 8 mm and 10 mm) and a countersink bit
Steel rule, try square, scriber, centre punch and hammer
Cutting fluid, a deburring tool and a chip brush
photos: The group doing the pre-start checks, with the check sheet
A plate marked out and centre punched
The plate clamped in the machine vice on packing
A member drilling, with the guard down and a watcher at the emergency stop
A finished plate with the holes drilled, countersunk and deburred
A rule laid against a finished plate to show the hole positions
The drill and table cleaned, with the tools put away
checklist: Wore safety glasses and no gloves near the drill, with sleeves, rings and hair secured
Took part in the pre-start checks (guard, emergency stop, table, chuck, belt cover)
Marked out and centre punched the holes accurately
Clamped the work securely on packing and never held it by hand
Chose a suitable speed for each drill and isolated the machine before any belt change
Removed the chuck key before starting, every time
Drilled pilot and final holes with a steady feed and cutting fluid, easing off at break-through
Holes in the right places (within the drawing's tolerance, about ±0.5 mm), countersunk and deburred
Cleared chips with a brush only after the drill had stopped, and left the machine clean
safety: Never hold the work by hand: clamp it in the machine vice or to the table
Do not wear gloves near the turning drill; remove rings and watches and tie back hair
Remove the chuck key before switching on
Switch off and isolate before changing the belt or freeing a jammed drill
Chips are sharp and hot: clear them with a brush only when the drill has stopped

practical2.title: Cut bar to length on a sawing machine and finish the ends on a pedestal grinder
practical2.brief: As a group, cut a set of parts to the assessor's cutting list and finish them on the pedestal grinder. The cutting list is 10 pieces of 40 mm × 6 mm mild steel flat bar, each 150 mm long: 2 pieces for each member (in a group of 4, members take turns to cut the extra pieces). Use the Centre's horizontal bandsaw or power hacksaw. First, as a group, carry out and record the pre-start checks on the saw (blade, tension, guards, vice, coolant) and on the grinder (wheel, guards, eye shield, work rest gap), with the machine isolated for any check that needs it. Then each member: (1) measures and marks their pieces from a square end, allowing for the width of the cut; (2) clamps the bar, supports the long end and cuts each piece; (3) deburrs the ends and grinds a small 45° chamfer on the two corners at one end of each piece on the pedestal grinder; (4) checks each piece for length and squareness with a rule and square; (5) marks the pieces with their initials. Photograph each stage and add the photos to the group's practical. Finish by cleaning both machines and the area.
materials: Mild steel flat bar, 40 mm × 6 mm, enough for 10 pieces of 150 mm
Horizontal bandsaw or power hacksaw with coolant, and a roller stand
Pedestal grinder with a water pot
Steel rule, try square, scriber and marker
Pre-start check sheets for the saw and the grinder
The cutting list from the assessor
photos: The group carrying out the pre-start checks on the saw and the grinder
A bar marked out and clamped in the saw vice, with the long end supported
A cut in progress, with the blade guide set close to the work
A member grinding a chamfer, with goggles on and the eye shield down
The finished pieces laid out in a row with a rule alongside
A square held against a cut end to show it is square
Both machines and the area cleaned
checklist: Wore safety glasses or goggles and boots, with no loose clothing, rings or gloves near moving parts
Took part in the pre-start checks and recorded them on the check sheet
Measured and marked from a square end, allowing for the width of the cut
Clamped the bar tightly, supported the long end and set the blade guide close
Let the blade feed down steadily without forcing it
Checked the work rest gap and stood to one side when starting the grinder
Ground the chamfers on the face of the wheel with light pressure, cooling the work in water
Pieces within about 1 mm of 150 mm long, with ends square and deburred
Switched off, let the machines stop, then cleaned them and the area
safety: Only use a machine you have been trained on, and follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
Keep the guards in place; adjust the blade guide or work rest only with the machine switched off and isolated
Never grind on the side of a straight wheel: use its face
Cut pieces are sharp and can be hot: handle them carefully and deburr them
Keep the floor clear of offcuts and wipe up coolant spills at once
